co_durango.blurb: Durango sits in the San Juan Mountains of southwest Colorado, and most of its climbing is a short drive from town. Bouldering is the biggest share, led by the blocks of Sailing Hawks, with sport and trad close behind and a little ice and mixed in winter. Roped climbs cluster between 5.8 and 5.12, with a solid supply of 5.10 and 5.11, and boulder problems run from easy up to double-digit V grades. The rock varies by area: limestone at Cascade Canyon and the steep sport wall at Golf Wall, sandstone boulders at Turtle Lake, granite around Lemon Reservoir, and a remote alpine quartzite setting at Vallecito Crags. Cascade Canyon turns into an ice park in winter, and the sandstone boulders can be climbed through much of the year.

mi_upper_peninsula.blurb: Michigan's Upper Peninsula is a big, spread-out region where the climbing centres on Marquette, with further pockets around Iron Mountain, the Copper Country and Munising. Bouldering makes up well over half of the climbs, and the roped routes are a mix of sport, trad and top rope, mostly between 5.6 and 5.11. Around Marquette the stone ranges from sandstone slopes and granite boulders to coastal rock and mountaintop slabs, many with views over Lake Superior. Winter adds a serious ice scene: the frozen Superior shoreline builds blue ice, and Munising is regarded as the Midwest's ice destination, mostly in the WI3 to WI5 range. Rock climbing is a spring, summer and fall activity.

wa_north_bend_vicinity.blurb: North Bend lies along I-90 at the western foot of the Cascades, roughly 45 minutes from Seattle, which makes it the city's after-work crag zone. Sport climbing dominates by a wide margin, with a strong boulder presence and a small amount of trad and mixed. Grades concentrate between 5.9 and 5.12, with plenty of moderates and a thin top end into the 5.13s and 5.14. The Exit 38 walls hold the largest share, with a beginner slab alongside steeper, harder faces, while Exit 32 near Little Si and the Exit 34 Middle Fork and Taylor River zone round out the picture. Climbing is often possible from about April through December, with rain the main limit. Trees keep some faces damp longer, and the busiest walls fill up on weekends.

ca_northeast_california.blurb: Northeast California is a broad swath of the Shasta Cascade, stretching from the Trinity Alps side across to the Nevada line and south to Lassen, with Mount Shasta as its centrepiece. The climbing is scattered across many small areas rather than one big hub. Bouldering is the largest share, followed by trad and sport, plus some alpine climbing, and most roped routes fall between 5.8 and 5.12. Rock types differ from place to place: limestone and rhyolite hold much of the sport climbing, while Castle Crags is granite, with spires, domes and walls up to several hundred feet and mostly trad lines. Doyle is the main bouldering zone, and Lassen offers high-country crags with big views.

az_prescott_area.blurb: Prescott is a mid-elevation town in central Arizona, around 5,300 feet, and it is loaded with granite. Trad is the largest roped share, with bouldering and sport next and a bit of top rope. Grades centre on 5.9 to 5.11, with enough easier routes for newcomers and a handful of hard ones above 5.12, and the boulder problems stretch well into double-digit V grades. The Granite Dells are rounded, sometimes grainy desert granite with the most routes, while Granite Mountain offers fine-grained white granite cracks and multi-pitch lines in a quiet wilderness setting. Sullivan's Canyon is basalt, and Thumb Butte also climbs on pocketed basalt. The town is a handy escape from Flagstaff's cold or the lower desert's heat.

qc_15_laurentides.blurb: The Laurentides are a region of hills, valleys and low mountains in Quebec, and the village of Val-David has long been the heart of Quebec climbing, a place that grew into a teaching ground for the sport. Trad and sport are about equally common, with a large amount of bouldering and a modest winter ice scene. Roped routes run mostly from 5.7 up to 5.12, with a good spread of moderates and a few harder sport lines. Val-David holds the biggest concentration of climbs, followed by Montagne d'Argent and Weir, and many smaller crags are spread across the region. Climbing is possible on both rock and ice, though the character varies a lot between the established cliffs and the lesser-visited ones.
